scope: Official-source research for a reported two-unit San Francisco property. Source verification does not authenticate any private lease, resident, address, ownership, or payment record.

sources.title: Annual Rent Increase for 3/1/26–2/28/27 Announced
sources.evidence: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
sources.verification_note: Agency announcement published January 14, 2026. It also specifies multiplication of base rent by .016. This is not a property-specific authorization.

sources.title: Allowable Annual Rent Increases — historical schedule
sources.evidence: Historical schedule includes annual percentages by effective-date interval, including 1.6% for March 1, 2026–February 28, 2027.
sources.verification_note: Use the rate applicable to the proposed effective date, not simply the date the notice is prepared. Historical percentages are not automatically available as banked increases.

sources.title: Learn About Rent Increases in San Francisco
sources.evidence: Guidance explains base rent, annual-increase timing, no rounding up, required notice, licensing, and protection for certain added occupants.
sources.verification_note: Read alongside the ordinance and Rule 4.12. Some summary examples have apparent date inconsistencies; do not use those examples to override the operative rule.

sources.title: Learn About San Francisco Rental Laws
sources.evidence: Coverage depends on the unit and applicable exemptions, not merely the neighborhood or ZIP code.
sources.verification_note: The reported 1940 construction year is consistent with an older building but does not establish coverage. Exact address/APN, unit records, exemptions, subsidy terms, and Rent Board history were not supplied.

sources.title: San Francisco Administrative Code § 37.3 — Rent Limitations
sources.publisher: City and County of San Francisco / American Legal Publishing
sources.evidence: Subsection (a)(1) limits the ordinary annual increase to 60% of the published CPI increase, never greater than 7%, subject to licensing. Subsection (a)(2) authorizes banking subject to § 37.15. Subsection (b) requires a written breakdown and states that a nonconforming increase is null and void.
sources.verification_note: Official publisher identified by SF.gov. Inspected subsections (a)(1)–(2), notice provisions, additional-occupant protection, Costa-Hawkins provisions, and partial-occupancy-change limitation. The page includes subsequent chapter sections; relevant section boundaries were checked.

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations — Part IV, Rules 4.10 and 4.12
sources.evidence: Rule 4.12 adds unused annual percentages without compounding; prohibits rounding up; permits a rent increase only once in any twelve-month period; and calls for disclosure of the banked portion and underlying dates.
sources.verification_note: The rules index identifies amendments through January 13, 2026. Rule 4.12 states that omission of the banking disclosure alone does not render an increase null and void; this does not displace the ordinance's other notice requirements. No cumulative banking cap appears in the inspected rule or § 37.3(a)(2); pending proposals are not treated as enacted law.

sources.title: Banked Rent Increases
sources.evidence: Banking can survive a sale but does not create a new tenancy or erase the existing tenancy's history.
sources.verification_note: Flagged wording discrepancy: the summary refers to 24 full months while Rule 4.12 uses a twelve-month increase-frequency rule. This project follows the primary rule and recommends no banked amount without a verified history.

sources.title: Rent Board Housing Inventory
sources.evidence: The Rent Board maintains a Housing Inventory and an online portal for required unit information.
sources.verification_note: No exact address or APN was available, so no property-specific inventory lookup or compliance finding was made.

sources.title: Sec. 37.15 — Reporting Obligations; Licensing
sources.evidence: Annual reporting is due March 1, including smaller properties. A license in substantial compliance is required for annual and banked increases; a suspended license prevents collection of those increases during noncompliance.
sources.verification_note: Restoration is prospective under the agency guidance. License status and reporting history for this property remain unverified.

sources.title: Landlord Petitions and Passthroughs
sources.evidence: Certain increases require a petition before notice; others require prescribed worksheets. Filing petitions is free. The Rent Board does not arbitrate ordinary rental-agreement breaches outside the Rent Ordinance.
sources.verification_note: No petition, certification, approved passthrough, or supporting expense record was supplied. None is assumed.

sources.title: Operating and Maintenance Expense Petitions — Topic 322
sources.evidence: An O&M petition may support an additional base-rent increase of up to 7% if the required expense comparison and other conditions are proved. Debt service is excluded, and specified ownership-related costs are disallowed.
sources.verification_note: This is a petition ceiling, not an automatic annual allowance. The guidance describes allocation across all units, including commercial units, and tenant objections/hardship relief. No eligibility or amount is established here.

sources.title: Special Circumstances Petitions Based on Rents for Comparable Units — Topic 323
sources.evidence: The mere fact that a long-standing tenant is paying significantly less than market rent is not considered an extraordinary circumstance.
sources.verification_note: A special-circumstances petition requires proof of extraordinary circumstances and reasonably comparable units; filing must precede notice. A long tenancy or a market benchmark alone is not a sufficient reason.

sources.title: Sec. 37.10C — Use and Sale of Algorithmic Devices Prohibited
sources.evidence: The ordinance prohibits specified revenue-management devices using nonpublic competitor rent or occupancy information to recommend rents or occupancy levels. Public aggregated reports without recommendations are excluded.
sources.verification_note: Added in 2024 and amended in 2025. No pricing software or competitor-data sharing is established for this owner. This dashboard uses public official data and transparent arithmetic.

sources.title: Report an Unlawful Rent Increase or Request Review of Your Rent History
sources.evidence: Tenants may request review of an unlawful increase or rent history using the Rent Board's petition process, with leases, notices, and payment evidence.
sources.verification_note: The agency describes free filing, no filing time limit for this petition, and an administrative-law-judge hearing. This is a route for independent challenge, not evidence that a violation occurred.

sources.title: Speak to a Rent Board Counselor
sources.evidence: Rent Board counselors provide free information; counselors do not provide legal advice. Telephone: 415-252-4600.
sources.verification_note: No counselor or attorney was contacted on the user's behalf in this session.

sources.title: Rent Board Referral Listing
sources.evidence: The directory lists the San Francisco Tenants Union, Housing Rights Committee of SF, Open Door Legal, Eviction Defense Collaborative, and Bar Association of San Francisco legal-help resources.
sources.verification_note: The Rent Board states it cannot refer individual attorneys. Eligibility and availability must be confirmed with each organization. No listed organization has reviewed or endorsed this project.

sources.title: Evictions in San Francisco
sources.publisher: City and County of San Francisco
sources.evidence: San Francisco requires just cause for covered evictions and describes protections for replacement or added occupants. The Eviction Defense Collaborative assists with eviction notices, summons, and complaints.
sources.verification_note: EDC's eviction-defense service is not represented here as a landlord-side rent-review service.

sources.title: Rent Ordinance — current publication index
sources.evidence: The index identifies an ordinance compilation amended November 2, 2026 and links the amendment list and compilation.
sources.verification_note: The compilation carries an administrative-convenience disclaimer. American Legal is the official publisher linked by the City. Recent listed amendments were checked for changes to the rent-limitation provisions relied on here.

sources.title: List of Rent Ordinance Amendments — November 2, 2026
sources.publisher: City and County of San Francisco
sources.evidence: Recent entries include Ordinance 3-26 affecting § 37.3, Ordinances 99-26 and 207-26 affecting Board composition/terms, and the 2024–2025 algorithmic-device amendments.
sources.verification_note: The final inspected entries do not show a new cumulative banking cap. This is a scoped check, not a representation that every unrelated eviction or administrative provision was exhaustively analyzed.

sources.title: California Civil Code § 827
sources.evidence: For the residential rent changes covered by the statute, notice is at least 30 days when the combined increases over the preceding 12 months do not exceed 10%, and at least 90 days when they exceed 10%. The statute specifies personal or mail service.
sources.verification_note: The relevant percentage comparison uses the rent in effect 12 months before the proposed effective date. Lease terms, local requirements, and any assistance-program requirements still require review. Email or text alone is not treated as statutory service.

sources.title: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1013
sources.evidence: The referenced mail-service extension is five calendar days within California, ten calendar days elsewhere in the United States, and twenty calendar days outside the United States; qualifying overnight delivery adds two court days.
sources.verification_note: Apply only through the incorporating notice statute and the actual service method. The calculator's overnight option is a conservative calendar-day planning buffer, not a court-day adjudication.

sources.title: California Civil Code § 1947.12 — Tenant Protection Act rent cap
sources.evidence: For covered properties, the cap is the lower of 5% plus the applicable CPI change or 10%, using the lowest lawful rent during the preceding 12 months, with no more than two increments for a continuing tenant. Exemptions and notice requirements apply.
sources.verification_note: The owner-occupied two-unit exemption has specific principal-residence, continuing-occupancy, and non-ADU conditions. Corporate/LLC ownership can affect a different exemption. Do not infer an exemption from unit count or ownership label alone.

sources.title: California Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482)
sources.evidence: The agency identifies a maximum 8.8% for state-covered increases effective August 1, 2026 through July 31, 2027; units subject to the local rent-increase limit retain that local limit.
sources.verification_note: The state maximum is not an alternative the owner may choose for a confirmed SF rent-controlled unit.

sources.title: California Civil Code § 1942.5 — Retaliation
sources.evidence: The statute restricts retaliatory rent increases and other adverse actions following protected tenant activity and habitability complaints, with a good-faith written-ground procedure and civil remedies.
sources.verification_note: The statutory presumption and its conditions are not a universal safe harbor after 180 days. Tenant activity, repair requests, communications, and the owner's actual reasons are unknown.

sources.title: Fair Housing and Housing Discrimination
sources.evidence: Housing protections cover discrimination in rental terms and conditions and retaliation based on protected characteristics or protected activity.
sources.verification_note: A policy applied to both units is not automatically nondiscriminatory. Protected-class facts were neither requested nor inferred.

sources.title: California Business and Professions Code § 16729
sources.evidence: The statute addresses specified uses or distribution of competitors' nonpublic competitively sensitive data in pricing algorithms and related pricing conduct.
sources.verification_note: Read together with SF § 37.10C. No evidence establishes that this owner uses a prohibited device or shares competitor data.

sources.title: Fair Housing Act — Rights and Obligations
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
sources.evidence: The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, and disability.
sources.verification_note: This source supports civil-rights review, not a universal federal rent percentage. Subsidy or other federal program status is unknown and must be checked separately.

sources.title: 24 CFR § 100.65 — Discrimination in terms and conditions
sources.evidence: The regulation prohibits discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of dwelling rental and in related services or facilities because of a protected characteristic.
sources.verification_note: Official published CFR PDF was inspected; the unofficial continuously updated eCFR was used only as a navigation aid.

sources.title: Justice Department Reaches Proposed Consent Decree with Pinnacle
sources.evidence: The September 4, 2026 announcement describes a proposed consent decree concerning algorithmic pricing and competitively sensitive information.
sources.verification_note: A proposed decree is not a final adjudication of liability and is not evidence about this property or owner. Corporate ownership alone does not establish unlawful pricing.

sources.title: FY 2027 San Francisco, CA HUD Metro FMR Area — all bedroom sizes
sources.publisher: HUD Office of Policy Development and Research
sources.evidence: FY 2027 FMRs: efficiency $2,574; one-bedroom $3,003; two-bedroom $3,697; three-bedroom $4,832; four-bedroom $5,439. The area comprises Marin, San Francisco, and San Mateo Counties.
sources.verification_note: These are gross-rent, housing-assistance benchmarks for the entire metropolitan FMR area, not ZIP 94122 asking rents, subject-unit appraisals, or lawful rent ceilings. The subject bedroom counts are unknown.

sources.title: HUD Small Area Fair Market Rents — ZIP 94122, FY 2026 service record
sources.publisher: HUD Office of Policy Development and Research
sources.evidence: The record with ID 94122 and HUD_CODE METRO41860MM7360 reports FY 2026 SAFMRs of $2,280 (0BR), $2,730 (1BR), $3,310 (2BR), $4,230 (3BR), and $4,380 (4BR).
sources.verification_note: The parent HUD service is explicitly labeled FY 2026 and its data edit timestamp is October 1, 2025. These values are historical as of November 6, 2026, not FY 2027 values. The populated ZIP field is ID; ZCTA_ID is null in this related table. FY 2027 ZIP values are left blank.

sources.title: Small Area Fair Market Rents — FY 2027 lookup and service metadata
sources.publisher: HUD Office of Policy Development and Research
sources.kind: Official dataset index and service metadata
sources.evidence: HUD identifies FY 2027 as the current lookup year. The linked ArcGIS service metadata identifies the available service as FY 2026.
sources.verification_note: The FY 2027 spreadsheet endpoint failed during retrieval and the lookup is interactive. No FY 2027 ZIP value was inferred from the metropolitan schedule or from FY 2026 data.

sources.title: 24 CFR § 888.113 — Fair market rents: methodology
sources.evidence: FMRs estimate rent plus utilities, excluding telephone, and are generally set at the 40th percentile of standard-quality recent-mover gross rents, subject to the regulation's adjustments.
sources.verification_note: A percentile benchmark is not a rent-control ceiling or an appraisal of either reported unit. The official published PDF controls the citation; eCFR was used for readable navigation.
